overview: FCG.NZ IS THE CO-OPERATIVE SHARE ITSELF, not the Fonterra Shareholders' Fund — a critically important distinction. FCG.NZ shares are held on the Fonterra Shareholders' Market, a restricted market where ownership and trading are generally limited to current and former supplying farmers, sharemilkers, contract milkers and farm lessors under the co-operative's constitution and Flexible Shareholding rules; an ordinary outside retail or institutional investor most likely CANNOT buy FCG.NZ and would instead need to buy the separate, freely-tradeable Fonterra Shareholders' Fund units (FSF.NZ). FCG shares carry full voting rights (one member, one vote, regardless of shareholding size) and elect the co-operative's board, whereas FSF units carry no vote. Fonterra Co-operative Group is the world's largest dairy exporter, collecting roughly 1.5-1.6bn kgMS of milk annually from ~8,000 New Zealand farming families and processing it for global export. Following the 31-Mar-2026 sale of its global Mainland/Consumer business to Lactalis for NZ$4.22bn, Fonterra is now a focused B2B dairy Ingredients and Foodservice exporter selling into more than 100 countries, with FY2025 Total Group revenue of roughly NZ$24-26bn and profit after tax of ~NZ$1.08bn. A NZ$2.00/share tax-free capital return (~NZ$3.2bn, funded by Lactalis proceeds) was paid 14-Apr-2026 following farmer-shareholder approval.

business_model.summary: Fonterra collects NZ farmers' milk and processes it into dairy Ingredients (proteins, milk powders, cheese, casein sold via NZMP/MyNZMP to food manufacturers globally) and Foodservice products (UHT cream, butter, mozzarella, Anchor Food Professionals brand sold to bakeries, QSRs and food service operators, concentrated in Greater China and Southeast Asia). The single largest cost line is the Farmgate Milk Price paid to farmer-suppliers, which is set competitively against a notional efficient processor. Importantly, for FCG.NZ holders specifically (who are, by definition, the same farmers supplying the milk), the Farmgate Milk Price is not simply a cost eroding their investment — it is their principal farm income. A farmer holding FCG shares is paid a high milk price on the milk they supply even when that same high milk price compresses the co-op's reported earnings and share dividend; the two cash flows (milk payment plus dividend) partially offset each other, so the milk-price/earnings tension that is a genuine problem for outside FSF unit holders is much less of a problem — arguably closer to a natural hedge — for the farmer-shareholders who actually hold FCG. Revenue is transactional/commodity-linked rather than recurring/contractual, though a growing 'contracted sales book' and digital channels (MyNZMP, MyNZMP Link) provide some forward revenue visibility.

revenue_streams.name: Ingredients (NZMP proteins, milk powders, cheese, casein, butter/AMF)
Foodservice (Anchor Food Professionals, UHT cream, butter, mozzarella)
Consumer/Mainland Group (Anchor, Mainland, Western Star, Perfect Italiano, Kapiti brands)
revenue_streams.trend: divested 31-Mar-2026, no longer part of continuing operations

business_model.customer_type: B2B — global food & beverage manufacturers, foodservice operators, bakeries and QSR chains; virtually no direct B2C exposure post-Mainland divestment
business_model.geographic_mix: Greater China largest single market (Foodservice-led, historically ~$400m+ operating profit segment); Southeast Asia (fastest-growing Foodservice region); New Zealand (100% of milk collection and manufacturing base, ~11,500+ FTEs, 24 manufacturing sites); Europe, Americas and Rest of AMENA as smaller Ingredients-sales regions; exports to more than 100 countries in total

main_competitors: a2 Milk / Synlait (NZ dairy processors, partly competing for milk supply)
Lactalis (now also a strategic Ingredients customer post-Mainland sale)
US and EU dairy co-operatives/exporters benefiting from rising milk supply
Chinese domestic dairy producers (Yili, Mengniu) reducing China's import reliance
competitive_position.market_position: World's largest dairy exporter, historically responsible for roughly 30% of global cross-border dairy trade; dominant collector of New Zealand's pasture-based milk supply (1,565m kgMS forecast FY26 from ~8,120 NZ farms); #1 or top-tier position in global whole milk powder, and a leading position in Foodservice cream/butter/mozzarella supply into Greater China and Southeast Asia

moat_factors.factor: Scale and NZ pasture-based low-cost production
moat_factors.description: NZ's temperate climate enables largely grass-fed, lower-cost milk production versus grain-fed systems elsewhere, and Fonterra's collection/manufacturing network (24 NZ sites) provides scale economics competitors cannot easily replicate domestically

Long-standing relationships with strategic partners (e.g., logistics provider Kotahi) and application/innovation centres (6 in China) support reliable delivery into 100+ markets even amid geopolitical disruption

New Zealand Dairy Grass-Fed Administrative Standard (launched China, June 2025) and 96% grass-fed data underpin a premium quality/provenance positioning in Ingredients and Foodservice, notably in China and Southeast Asia

Flexible Shareholding requires supplying farmers to hold FCG shares proportional to milk supplied (1-4 shares per kgMS), tying the farmer base's own capital to continued supply and creating switching friction versus rival processors; this is a genuine structural anchor for milk-supply retention, distinct from being a competitive moat over rival processors' products

weaknesses: Fixed NZ milk supply ceiling (~1.5-1.6bn kgMS) constrains volume growth; the company competes hard against Open Country Dairy and others just to retain/attract NZ farmer suppliers
Commodity/cyclical earnings exposed to global milk supply swings (US, EU, and NZ production growth has driven the FY2026/27 milk price forecast down materially)
Loss of the higher-margin, brand-differentiated Consumer/Mainland portfolio removes a diversification buffer and a direct-to-consumer brand moat
China import demand has structurally declined as domestic self-sufficiency has grown, reducing the value of Fonterra's largest historical market for milk powder
Manufacturing cost performance has recently run above strategic targets ($2.73/kgMS forecast vs $2.62 target in FY26), reflecting NZ input cost inflation and secondary processing costs

growth_drivers: Post-Mainland focus on higher-margin, less capital-intensive B2B Ingredients and Foodservice, with management targeting Group earnings to return to pre-divestment (FY25) levels by FY28
Foodservice expansion beyond Greater China into Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand) leveraging the Anchor Food Professionals brand and grass-fed positioning

Product mix shift toward high-value Advanced & Specialty Ingredients (proteins, functional whey, cheese) — Studholme advanced protein hub completed, first products Feb-2026; new Clandeboye butter line and Edendale UHT cream expansion (~late 2026) adding high-return capacity
Up to NZ$1 billion in further growth capital investment being assessed over 3-4 years across protein portfolio, butter/cream cheese, and site data/AI/automation
Digital sales channels (MyNZMP, MyNZMP Link) improving customer reach/contracted sales visibility in US/EU and reducing sales friction
Cost discipline and the multi-year ERP transformation (on track for completion late 2028, spend peaking FY26/FY27) targeted to structurally lower cash operating costs per kgMS
Organic milk expansion into the South Island, capturing a record ~$14.00/kgMS organic milk price premium
Capital return program (NZ$2.00/share tax-free capital return paid 14-Apr-2026, ~NZ$3.2bn) demonstrates capital discipline and may be followed by further returns depending on debt/earnings settings

business.risk: FCG.NZ is a restricted-transfer security most outside investors cannot buy
business.description: FCG shares trade on the Fonterra Shareholders' Market, a market restricted under Fonterra's constitution and Flexible Shareholding rules to current and former supplying farmers, sharemilkers, contract milkers and farm lessors. An ordinary retail or institutional investor is generally not eligible to hold or trade FCG shares at all; anyone reading this analysis as a prospective investment idea should note the practically investable NZX security for outside capital is the separate Fonterra Shareholders' Fund (FSF.NZ), not FCG.NZ. The FCG market is correspondingly thin and illiquid, with a narrow, captive buyer pool of farmer-shareholders rather than the broad market that prices FSF.NZ

China is Fonterra's largest single market but its dairy self-sufficiency has risen materially since 2018, reducing multi-year whole milk powder import volumes; Foodservice (UHT cream, butter, mozzarella) has partly offset this via demand from bakeries/QSR, but the historical ingredients export growth story into China cannot be assumed to continue

Divesting Consumer removes a higher-margin, less commodity-linked earnings stream (~$397m normalised discontinued-operations operating profit in FY25); Fonterra is now more concentrated in commodity-price-sensitive Ingredients earnings, at least until the promised FY28 earnings recovery materialises

Competing NZ processors (Open Country Dairy, Synlait, Westland) actively compete for farmer milk supply; Fonterra must continually enhance its farmer offering (advance rate flexibility, emissions incentives, shareholding requirement easing) to retain and grow its supplier base

CEO Miles Hurrell announced his resignation in March 2026 (serving a ~6-month notice period to around September 2026) shortly after completing the Mainland divestment and capital restructure; a new CEO search was ongoing as of mid-2026, creating leadership transition risk during the critical post-divestment strategy execution phase (Richard Allen, President Global Ingredients, has been acting as primary spokesperson through mid-2026)

financial.risk: Commodity price cyclicality flowing straight to earnings
financial.description: Global Dairy Trade (GDT) auction pricing for whole milk powder and other reference products directly drives both the Farmgate Milk Price (a farmer's income, but the co-op's cost) and Ingredients segment margins; GDT prices fell materially through mid-2026 (e.g., an 11% fall across reference products by July 2026, prompting a cut to the FY2026/27 milk price forecast), illustrating how quickly earnings assumptions can move. Note that for FCG holders (farmers) the income/dividend impact of a lower milk price is more directly offset by lower farm-gate receipts than for a pure outside investor

Net debt was ~NZ$2.6bn at FY25 and ~NZ$4.9bn at 1H-FY26 (elevated ahead of the Mainland transaction proceeds/capital return); Fonterra targets Debt-to-EBITDA below 3x and a 30-40% gearing ratio, but leverage moves with working capital and dividend/capital-return timing
Export-driven revenue is priced predominantly in USD while costs (Farmgate Milk Price, NZ operations) are in NZD; currency movements affect reported margins and the Farmgate Milk Price calculation

Because the buyer pool for FCG shares is restricted to farmers and former farmers, trading volumes and liquidity are structurally lower than a typical NZX-listed equity of comparable size, which can widen bid/ask spreads and increase price volatility around events like the co-operative's capital return

regulatory.description: New Zealand on-farm methane/emissions policy remains a live and evolving area (successor mechanisms to the abandoned He Waka Eke Noa proposal); any future on-farm emissions pricing or compliance cost increases would raise the cost base for Fonterra's supplying farmers and could indirectly pressure the Farmgate Milk Price and Fonterra's own Scope 1-3 targets (net zero by 2050, 2030 interim targets)

As an export-intensive business selling into 100+ countries, Fonterra is exposed to tariff actions, trade agreement changes and geopolitical disruption (management has explicitly flagged Middle East conflict risk to shipping and input costs, and broader 'geopolitical dynamics' risk to commodity prices and exchange rates)

Fonterra's Flexible Shareholding rules (minimum/maximum shares per kgMS supplied) and the separate Fonterra Shareholders' Fund cap are periodically revisited by farmer vote; a live proposal would cut the Fund cap to 10% of total shares and restrict future share-to-unit conversion to a farmer-only market. This is primarily a risk/consideration for Fund (FSF.NZ) unit holders whose float and liquidity would shrink further — for FCG co-operative shareholders it is arguably neutral-to-mildly-positive, since it retains more of the economic interest in Fonterra within the farmer-owned co-operative rather than leaking it to outside capital

macro.description: Rising milk production from the US, EU and NZ has been the primary driver of the FY2026/27 Farmgate Milk Price forecast cut (from $9.75 midpoint in May-2026 to $9.25 by July-2026); a structurally higher global supply environment would compress both milk price and Ingredients margins for an extended period

Adverse weather events during the 2025/26 season disrupted milk collections for some farmers despite overall record volumes; droughts or extreme weather in future seasons remain a direct volume risk given Fonterra's near-total reliance on NZ pasture-based supply

Long-run growth of plant-based and alternative-protein products is a slow-moving but persistent demand risk for traditional dairy ingredients, particularly in Western retail/consumer categories (less relevant to B2B Ingredients/Foodservice but a latent industry risk)

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Underlying global demand for dairy is viewed by management as structurally supported by population growth, a growing global middle class, and consumer trends toward out-of-home dining, healthy ageing and active living, but near-term global supply (US, EU, NZ production growth) is outpacing demand, driving GDT prices and the Farmgate Milk Price down through mid-to-late 2026
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — Fonterra's earnings and the Farmgate Milk Price are both direct functions of global commodity dairy prices (Global Dairy Trade auctions), making the business meaningfully cyclical despite the defensive nature of underlying dairy consumption
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — net debt (~NZ$2.6-4.9bn depending on period) means Fonterra carries meaningful interest expense; capital-intensive manufacturing investment programme also has some rate sensitivity via cost of debt funding
key_input_costs: Farmgate Milk Price (largest single cost, ~NZ$9.40-10.00/kgMS FY26 forecast range)
Global Dairy Trade reference product pricing (whole milk powder, skim milk powder, protein)

recent_developments.event: Fonterra cut its opening 2026/27 Farmgate Milk Price forecast to $9.25/kgMS (range $8.00-$10.50, down from $9.75 midpoint/$8.00-$11.00 range announced in May), citing an 11% GDT reference-product price fall since May amid strong global milk supply from the US and Europe outpacing demand

Q3 FY26 business update: Total Group operating profit YTD $1.8bn (+$103m YoY), underlying EPS 57c (vs 53c prior); FY26 full-year earnings guidance lifted and narrowed to 60-70 cents/share (from 50-65c); current-season Farmgate Milk Price narrowed to $9.60-$9.80/kgMS (midpoint $9.70, unchanged); opening 2026/27 milk price forecast set at $9.75/kgMS ($8.00-$11.00 range); record organic milk price midpoint of $14.00/kgMS announced; CEO commentary (Richard Allen) reaffirmed focus on growing high-value Ingredients and Foodservice post-divestment

Completed sale of Mainland Group (global Consumer and associated businesses: Anchor, Mainland, Fernleaf, Western Star, Perfect Italiano, Kapiti) to Lactalis for NZ$4.22bn, following 98.85% farmer shareholder approval at a 19-Feb-2026 special meeting and satisfaction of regulatory conditions

CEO Miles Hurrell announced his resignation after leading Fonterra since 2018 through the strategic reset and Mainland divestment; six-month notice period to ~September 2026; Chair Peter McBride said a new CEO would be appointed 'in the coming months'

Fonterra distributed NZ$3.9 billion in cash to shareholders and unit holders: a tax-free NZ$2.00/share capital return (~$3.2bn, funded by Lactalis sale proceeds) plus a fully imputed 40 cents/share interim distribution (24c ordinary interim dividend, up from 22c, plus a 16c special Mainland dividend representing 100% of Mainland's FY26 earnings while under Fonterra ownership); FSF.NZ's unit price fell from $8.40 (9-Apr-2026) to $6.38 (14-Apr-2026) reflecting the ex-distribution step-down, while FCG.NZ (the co-operative share) showed no equivalent step-down, trading ~$4.10-4.20 through March 2026 and rising to $4.55 in April 2026 — direct market confirmation that FCG and FSF are separate, differently-priced securities despite both referencing Fonterra's underlying performance

H1-FY26 (six months to 31-Jan-2026): Total Group profit after tax $750m (+$21m/+3% YoY), reported EPS 45c (up from 44c), normalised EPS 51c (up 4c YoY excluding $90m of Mainland divestment/separation costs); operating profit up from $1.1bn to $1.2bn on stronger in-market pricing and mix, particularly Foodservice in Southeast Asia and Greater China; net debt reduced from $5.5bn to $4.9bn; return on capital 11.2% (up from 10.4%), tracking within the FY26 10-12% target range

Farmer shareholder vote process: divestment approved by farmers (vote associated with the August-2025 announcement of the Lactalis deal), followed by a further 19-Feb-2026 special meeting where 98.85% of votes supported the capital return mechanics, clearing the way for Court approval and the April-2026 distribution. As FCG shareholders, farmers who supply Fonterra directly voted on and approved both the Mainland divestment and the capital return — full governance control that a Fund (FSF.NZ) unit holder does not have

guidance.as_of: Q3 FY2026 Business Update, 28 May 2026 (partially superseded by 12-Jul-2026 milk price update for the FOLLOWING season, FY2026/27)

items.notes: Lifted and narrowed from 50-65 cents (guided at H1-FY26 results, which itself had already been raised from an initial 45-65 cents range at FY25 results); reflects confidence in the Co-op's contracted sales position per Q3 FY26 update

Midpoint unchanged at $9.70 since the H1-FY26 result; range narrowed from the earlier $9.40-$10.00 given increased visibility late in the season; down from the record $10.16 final price in FY2025. This is direct farm income to FCG-holding farmer-shareholders, not just a co-op cost line

Cut from the opening $9.75/kgMS (range $8.00-$11.00) forecast given in May-2026, following an 11% fall in GDT reference-product prices amid strong global supply (US, Europe) outpacing demand; management flagged 'significant exposure to changes in commodity prices' given how early in the season sales contracting is
Reflects continued expansion of the organic milk programme, including into the South Island
Strategic target set from FY26 onward, above Fonterra's 5-year historical average; tracking within range at 1H-FY26
Debt-to-EBITDA target tightened (amended) from a prior looser target during FY25 to reflect a conservative balance sheet approach ahead of and after the Mainland divestment

FY25 full-year dividend of 57 cents was at the upper end of this policy range; H1-FY26 interim dividend of 24 cents (ordinary) plus a separate 16 cents special Mainland dividend (100% of Mainland FY26 earnings while owned); this dividend is paid identically per-share/per-unit to both FCG shareholders and FSF unit holders

items.target: Cash opex $1.12/kgMS (post-Mainland) and NZ manufacturing cash costs $2.62/kgMS by FY26 (strategic targets)
items.vs_prior: mixed — opex ahead of target ($0.98/kgMS actual vs $1.12 target at 1H-FY26), but NZ manufacturing costs behind target ($2.73/kgMS forecast vs $2.62 target)
items.notes: Company is 'reviewing its approach to lifting manufacturing cost performance' given higher input costs (lactose, secondary processing) despite record milk collection volumes

items.target: ~$980m FY26, ~$930m planned FY25 actual base; further ~$1bn of growth capex under review over next 3-4 years
items.notes: Includes Studholme advanced protein hub ($75m, completed), Clandeboye butter line ($75m, under construction), Edendale UHT cream expansion ($150m, ~complete late 2026), plus decarbonisation/electrification projects

items.target: Return Group earnings to FY25 (pre-divestment) levels
items.notes: Management's explicit medium-term target to offset the loss of Mainland Group earnings through growth in Ingredients/Foodservice plus cost efficiency

guidance.management_commentary: Following the Mainland divestment, then-CEO Miles Hurrell and (from Q3 update onward) Richard Allen (President, Global Ingredients, acting as primary spokesperson) reiterated that Fonterra is 'firmly focused on growing our high-value Ingredients and Foodservice businesses' as a leaner B2B dairy exporter. Management explicitly flagged heightened uncertainty from Middle East conflict risk (input costs, shipping disruption) and from rising global milk supply pressuring commodity prices; they cautioned that with the FY2026/27 sales book only lightly contracted this early in the season, Fonterra faces 'significant exposure to changes in commodity prices.' The Board has stated capital returns beyond the NZ$2.00/share Mainland-proceeds distribution will depend on future capital requirements, growth investment needs in Foodservice/Ingredients, and the Co-op's debt and earnings outlook, and has characterised the Mainland sale as 'likely to be the last major asset sale for Fonterra.'
guidance.note: Guidance and dividend/capital-return decisions are set by the Fonterra board, which is elected by and accountable to FCG co-operative shareholders (farmers) — i.e., holders of the ticker actually under research here have a direct vote in setting this guidance, unlike Fund (FSF.NZ) unit holders who receive the same per-share cash distributions but have no vote.

fcg_vs_fsf_note.summary: FCG.NZ and FSF.NZ are two separate, independently priced NZX-listed securities that both reference Fonterra Co-operative Group's performance but differ fundamentally in rights and eligible holders.
fcg_vs_fsf_note.fcg_nz: Fonterra Co-operative Group Limited co-operative shares. Held on the restricted Fonterra Shareholders' Market; ownership generally limited to current/former supplying farmers, sharemilkers, contract milkers and farm lessors under Flexible Shareholding rules. Carry full voting rights (elect the board, approve major transactions such as the Mainland divestment and capital return). ~1,609 million shares on issue. Price ~NZ$4.25 (10-Aug-2026).
fcg_vs_fsf_note.fsf_nz: Fonterra Shareholders' Fund units. A separate, open, freely tradeable managed investment scheme available to any investor (retail or institutional), listed on the NZX main board (and historically cross-listed). No voting rights in Fonterra Co-operative Group; investors elect only directors of the Fund's separate corporate Manager. Capped at 107,410,984 units on issue (unchanged FY24-H1FY26), with the distribution reinvestment plan currently suspended and a live proposal to cut the Fund cap further to 10% of total shares and restrict future share-to-unit conversion to a farmer-only market. Price ~NZ$7.05 (10-Aug-2026).
fcg_vs_fsf_note.why_prices_differ: The persistent price gap (NZ$4.25 for FCG vs NZ$7.05 for FSF as of 10-Aug-2026) reflects genuinely different buyer pools and rights, not measurement error: FSF trades in an open market accessible to all investors and carries a scarcity/liquidity premium plus the option value of eventual governance influence via any future capital-structure change, while FCG trades in a closed, thin market restricted to farmers, for whom the shareholding is bundled with (and partly a precondition of) their milk-supply relationship rather than a pure financial investment. The two prices also diverge visibly around cash events: on the 14-Apr-2026 capital return, FSF fell from $8.40 to $6.38 (the expected ~$2.02 step-down for the $2.00 capital return plus 40c distribution, since FSF's open-market price fully capitalises future distribution rights), while FCG showed no comparable step-down and instead rose modestly (~$4.10-4.20 in March 2026 to $4.55 in April 2026) — confirming FCG's restricted farmer market prices the co-operative relationship differently than FSF's open market prices the pure economic security.
fcg_vs_fsf_note.implication_for_this_analysis: Because FCG.NZ is presented here as the researched ticker, this analysis treats it as an operating-company equity analysis of Fonterra Co-operative Group. However, a general investor considering acting on this research should understand they most likely cannot purchase FCG.NZ directly and would need to consider FSF.NZ instead, which carries the same economic (dividend) exposure to Fonterra's results but no vote, a capped/thinning float, and a materially different (higher, and currently policy-uncertain) price.

bull_case: Post-Mainland Fonterra is a leaner, more focused B2B Ingredients and Foodservice exporter with less capital intensity and (management targets) improving margins, funded by NZ$4.22bn of Lactalis divestment proceeds and a materially reduced net debt position

Foodservice growth in Greater China and Southeast Asia (Anchor Food Professionals, UHT cream, butter, mozzarella) continues to outperform, supported by grass-fed provenance branding and an expanding footprint into Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand

FCG shareholders (farmers) hold full voting control of the co-operative and are economically hedged across the milk-price/earnings cycle — a high Farmgate Milk Price directly increases their farm income even when it compresses reported co-op earnings, unlike the position of a pure outside capital provider

Meaningful, tax-advantaged capital return already delivered (NZ$2.00/share paid April 2026) plus a stated 60-80% dividend payout policy provides a solid income return alongside a stable-to-improving Return on Capital (11.2% at 1H-FY26, within the 10-12% target range)

Multi-year investment in high-value Advanced & Specialty Ingredients capacity (Studholme, Clandeboye, Edendale) targets higher-margin protein/functional ingredients demand that is structurally growing in the US/EU, diversifying away from pure commodity milk powder, with an explicit management target to restore Group earnings to FY25 (pre-divestment) levels by FY28
bear_case: FCG.NZ is a restricted-transfer security that most outside investors cannot legally hold or trade — it is only tradeable by current/former supplying farmers on the closed Fonterra Shareholders' Market, so this is a largely uninvestable idea for a general investor, who would need to consider the differently-priced, non-voting FSF.NZ units instead

The FCG market is thin and illiquid relative to a typical NZX security of this size, given the narrow, captive farmer buyer pool, which can produce wider spreads and price behaviour that does not always track fundamentals cleanly

China, historically Fonterra's largest market, faces structurally declining import demand for milk powder as domestic self-sufficiency rises, eroding a multi-decade growth pillar even as Foodservice partially offsets the impact

Earnings are highly commodity-cyclical: the FY2026/27 Farmgate Milk Price forecast was already cut from $9.75 to $9.25/kgMS within two months (July 2026) as global milk supply from the US and Europe outpaced demand and GDT prices fell 11%, illustrating how quickly guidance and co-op earnings/dividends can move against holders (even if the milk-price side of that move is a partial offset for farmer-shareholders specifically)

Loss of the higher-margin, diversifying Mainland Consumer business removes an earnings buffer just as the company undergoes a CEO transition (Miles Hurrell's resignation, announced March 2026, with a new CEO still being recruited through mid-2026) during a critical period of post-divestment strategy execution
